source.title: Mixture of Experts Made Intrinsically Interpretable
source.authors: Xing-Yi Yang; Constantin Venhoff; Ashkan Khakzar; Christian Schroeder de Witt; P. Dokania; A. Bibi; P. Torr

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether width and activation sparsity relate to interpretability in trained transformer models, using chess-board-state metrics and an automated interpretation task rather than directly measuring superposition geometry.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on width, sparsity, and interpretability proxies. It also discusses feature superposition as an explanation, but does not directly measure overlapping directions, their angles, a sparsity-dependent geometric transition, or feature importance. Figure-only sweep values are recorded as figure-only or as the authors' stated aggregate trend. Auto-interpretability results concern individual hidden activations and do not establish feature spreading across neurons or SAE recovery.
record.test_reason: The paper is mainly an architecture paper (MoE-X). Its preliminary Study I does test, in trained 8-layer chess transformers, whether wider MLPs give more feature-aligned (less polysemantic) neurons, which the authors frame as superposition through capacity. Its SAE-splicing perplexity results bear on SAE completeness (V5). Most other rows compare the authors' own method with baselines and are not tests of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that width and sparsity are key to interpretability and that MoE-X (ReLU experts plus sparsity-aware routing) improves interpretability while matching dense performance. They attribute the width and sparsity effects to reduced superposition only as a hypothesis, without measuring it.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains transformer language models and MoE variants and measures chess BSP interpretability and automated interpretation detection. It does not use the original toy-model intervention or measure feature-direction geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: Width scaling method (changing d versus α) affects coverage; sparsity level matters, and extreme sparsity is not always best. The reported layer also matters: chess interpretability peaks at layer 6 in the 8-layer model, and the study evaluates selected middle layers for other depths.

fits_no_version.finding: Imposing activation sparsity (ReLU or Top-k) typically raises neuron BSP coverage, with larger gains in larger models. Extreme sparsity is not always best.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation sparsity in MLP neurons increases neuron-level interpretability in transformers.

fits_no_version.finding: Auto-interp detection accuracy: MoE-X Small matches GPT-2+SAE and MoE-X Medium exceeds it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MoE-X expert neurons are as interpretable as SAE latents by LLM-scored detection.

fits_no_version.finding: MoE and ablation comparisons of coverage and reconstruction (Tables 1, 3, 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Wide and sparse MoE layers with ReLU experts and sparsity-aware routing yield more interpretable neurons than dense or other 'interpretable' architectures.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (2025), as stated in the supplied metadata; the text identifies itself as a preprint.
record.problems: The study uses chess board-state coverage and reconstruction as interpretability proxies rather than measuring polysemanticity or superposition geometry directly. Several sweep results are available only in figures. The auto-interpretability score uses LLM-generated explanations and an LLM scorer; the supplied text gives 95% confidence intervals but not their numeric values. It does not test feature importance, sharing versus dedicated dimensions, or SAE feature stability and canonicality.
record.rows_left_out: No otherwise qualifying reported result was omitted. Figure 5's model-size curves are not transcribed as separate numeric rows because the text supplies only aggregate comparisons; the stated aggregate findings are covered in the authors' conclusion and the relevant width/SAE rows.

untested.parts: All of it: no toy model, geometry, or sparsity-dependent transition.
Feature importance and the dedicated-versus-shared allocation. Superposition is only hypothesized, not measured.
The SAE is used only as a baseline. Whether features are spread across neurons is not measured.
Stability, canonicality, and feature-level completeness beyond the downstream loss cost.

missing.what: SAE loss recovery on chess of about 96%, versus 100% for MoE-X
missing.locator: Section 5.1, 'MoE-X beats SAE with Greater Faithfulness'

missing.what: Dense GPT-2 neuron coverage and reconstruction versus width α∈{4,8,16} at d=512 (figure-only)

record.verdict_notes: Primarily a method paper; superposition is invoked as motivation. Only the Study I width sweep (V2) and the SAE perplexity cost (V5) bear on versions, both indirectly. Interpretability is a chess BSP proxy measured at layer 6, chosen because the score peaks there. The V5 verdict rests on one SAE trained by the authors.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test toy networks with more sparse features than dimensions, or measure overlapping nearly orthogonal directions, regular geometry, or a sparsity-dependent transition.
It tests width and sparsity against interpretability proxies, but does not directly measure feature competition, which features receive dedicated dimensions, or whether importance determines sharing.
The study does not test whether polysemanticity arises for reasons other than capacity pressure.

The study evaluates SAE and model interpretability on chess board-state properties, but does not establish that real-model features are generally spread across many neurons or that an SAE recovers the model's full feature set.
The study compares SAE-based interpretability and reports a performance cost, but does not test feature stability across training, contexts, or methods, nor whether SAE features are canonical units.
The study does not test whether represented features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional subspaces.

relationships.condition: 8-layer GPT-2-like chess models, MLP width sweep, layer-6 neurons
relationships.reason: Neuron BSP coverage rises as width D=αd increases (r1). This is consistent with capacity limiting monosemanticity, though measured by a proxy with figure-only values.
relationships.display_finding: Neuron BSP coverage rose as MLP width D = αd increased. This fits capacity limiting monosemanticity, though BSP coverage is only a proxy measure.

relationships.condition: GPT-2 Small with a post-res layer-8 SAE (size 4096), four language-modeling datasets
relationships.reason: Splicing in the SAE raises perplexity on all four datasets (r19-r22). The authors say the SAE fails to capture all crucial features, so it is incomplete.

source_check.condition: GPT-2 Small with a post-res layer-8 SAE (size 4096), four language-modeling datasets
source_check.reason: Table 2 supports the incompleteness finding attributed to r19–r22: GPT-2 Small versus GPT-2 Small with SAE perplexities are 22.83 versus 31.60 on OpenWeb, 32.71 versus 38.21 on LAMBADA, 49.89 versus 55.33 on WikiText103, and 44.36 versus 49.16 on WikiText2. tranche.reason: The preliminary experiments extend the capacity/interpretability question to trained transformer language models on chess, a new setting beyond the original toy networks.

source_check.notes: The authors-conclusion paraphrase is supported. Preserve the source's D/d inconsistency as an explicit caveat; BSP coverage averages the best single-feature classifier F1 for each board-state property and does not directly measure superposition.

statements.correction: Section 3: increasing d and α increases BSP coverage; scaling α performs better than scaling d. Layer-6 MLP hidden activations in an 8-layer GPT-2-like chess model. Explicit prose scores: (α=16, d=512), coverage 0.53; (α=4, d=512)+SAE, coverage 0.45.
statements.problem: The chess-model result and layer/depth conditions are correct, but coverage values are not exclusively figure-only.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Width and sparsity sweeps, and the chess MoE comparisons
reader_labels.reason: The study reports improved interpretability proxies with increasing width and typical sparsification, and higher coverage/reconstruction for Switch and MoE-X than the dense reference (r1, r3, r11, r12, r16). These are indirect proxies, not direct measurements of capacity competition.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: ReLU alone falls below the GELU reference on both tabled interpretability metrics, and the paper states that the most extreme sparsity does not always yield the best interpretability; outcomes therefore depend on the specific design and sparsity level (r3, r5, r14, r15).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Chess BSP coverage comparison with the stated SAE baseline
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports an SAE BSP coverage score of 0.45, while the wider model scores 0.53; this shows that the SAE baseline recovers some board-state structure, though it does not establish general feature recovery in LLMs (r2, r18).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: GPT-2 Small with SAE on the four reported language-modeling datasets
reader_labels.reason: Perplexity is higher with SAE than for GPT-2 Small on all four datasets, and the authors say SAE fails to capture all crucial features; this challenges completeness in the tested setup but says nothing about canonicality or stability (r19-r22).
